rows.question: i have [[Hardened Scales]] and [[Doubling Season]] and cast ballista for X=2. how many counters does it come in with? do i get to pick the order or is it timestamps
rows.expected_answer: You choose the order and the best answer is 6. Walking Ballista's 'enters with X +1/+1 counters' is a replacement effect (614.1c, 614.12), and Hardened Scales and Doubling Season are further replacement effects modifying the same event. When multiple replacement effects apply to the same event, the affected permanent's controller picks which applies first (616.1), and since none of the special priorities in 616.1a-d apply, any may be chosen (616.1e). Each effect applies only once to the event (614.5). Apply Scales first (2 -> 3), then Season doubles (3 -> 6). Timestamps are irrelevant for replacement effects; that is the layer system for continuous effects.

outcome.answer:
You get **6** if you order them right. Both are replacement effects modifying the same event (Walking Ballista entering with 2 +1/+1 counters), so as the affected permanent's controller you choose the order to apply them — timestamps don't matter here (`616.1`, `616.1e`).

**Walking Ballista** "enters with X +1/+1 counters on it," so with X=2 the base event is 2 counters. Apply **Hardened Scales** first (2+1 = 3), then **Doubling Season** doubles that to 6. Apply Doubling Season first (2×2 = 4), then Scales adds one, for 5. Scales-first is strictly better.

Both do apply to counters a permanent enters with: Scales says "If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one +1/+1 counters are put on it instead," and Doubling Season "affects permanents that enter with counters." Each effect only gets one shot at the event, so there's no loop (`614.5`).
citations: rule 616.1: "If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or t…"
rule 616.1e: "Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen."
rule 614.5: "A replacement effect doesn’t invoke itself repeatedly; it gets only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that may replace that event."
oracle 4b515bb0-f275-4400-8032-3173b799ab40#0: "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it."

ruling a1f3da21-af6d-450e-bf0b-985d158418e6/636b245ed2960105: "If two or more effects attempt to modify how many counters would be put on a creature you control, you choose the order to apply those effects, no matter who controls the sources of those effects."
ruling 01546b7d-a233-4176-8843-d732074dc5b6/30e1af27509ea83b: "Doubling Season affects permanents that enter with counters."

rows.question: opp cast [[Blood Moon]] while i have all three tron lands out. do i still get my 7 mana from urza's? can i tap tower for 3 colorless or is it just a Mountain now
rows.expected_answer: Tron is off. Blood Moon is a type-changing effect (layer 4, 613.1d) that sets each nonbasic land's subtype to Mountain. Per 305.7, a land whose subtype is set to a basic land type loses its old land types (so it is no longer an Urza's land), loses all abilities from its rules text (the colorless mana ability), and gains only '{T}: Add {R}'. Each Urza's land is a plain Mountain that taps for one red mana; Tower does not produce three because it no longer has that ability and the others no longer have the Urza's subtype. They are still nonbasic (305.8), so Blood Moon keeps affecting them.

outcome.answer:
No Tron mana at all. **Blood Moon**'s "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" sets each nonbasic land's subtype, and per `305.7` such a land "no longer has its old land type. It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type." So **Urza's Tower**, **Urza's Mine** and **Urza's Power Plant** all lose the Urza's/Tower/Mine/Power-Plant land types and lose their "{T}: Add {C}. If you control…" abilities entirely; each is just a Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}." Tapping all three gives you {R}{R}{R}, not 7 (or even 3 colorless).

Double whammy on the check, too: the Tron ability "checks for land types, not the names of other permanents you control" — and those land types are gone — but you don't even get that far, since the ability itself is stripped. They're still nonbasic, still named Urza's Tower, etc.; Blood Moon doesn't change names or supertypes.
citations: rule 305.7: "If an effect sets a land’s subtype to one or more of the basic land types, the land no longer has its old land type. It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any c…"

ruling 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae/de7b24c7cfc8d0d2: "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability \"{T}: Add {R}.\""
ruling 32fbb638-ab14-4e8b-a07a-d4c44e3496f2/67514ffa8ee40389: "The ability checks for land types, not the names of other permanents you control."

rows.question: follow up: what if I play [[Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth]] AFTER the moon is already down? urborg has the later timestamp so shouldn't it make everything a Swamp too? my friend says no
rows.expected_answer: Your friend is right. Both effects are layer 4 type-changing effects (613.1d). Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's (613.8a): applying Blood Moon makes Urborg a Mountain and strips its rules-text ability (305.7), which removes the existence of Urborg's effect. When a dependency exists it overrides timestamps (613.8), so Blood Moon applies first no matter which entered later (613.8b). Urborg is just a Mountain with '{T}: Add {R}' and nothing becomes a Swamp. (Any actual basic Swamps you control are still Swamps because Blood Moon only affects nonbasic lands.)

outcome.answer:
Your friend is right: nothing becomes a Swamp. **Blood Moon** reads "Nonbasic lands are Mountains," and **Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth** is a nonbasic (Legendary) land, so Blood Moon sets Urborg's subtype to Mountain. Per `305.7`, a land whose subtype is set to a basic land type "loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type" — so Urborg no longer has "Each land is a Swamp in addition to its other land types" and never generates that effect at all.

Timestamps don't save it, because dependency overrides timestamp order (`613.8`). Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's — applying Blood Moon "would change the text or the existence of the first effect" (`613.8a`) — while Blood Moon doesn't depend on Urborg (it applies to all nonbasic lands either way). So Urborg's effect waits to apply until after Blood Moon has applied (`613.8b`), by which point it doesn't exist. Scryfall says the same about the identical Magus of the Moon case: "it won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply."

Urborg just sits there as a nonbasic Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}".

rows.question: my goyf has two +1/+1 counters on it and I just giant growthed it. opponent [[Clone]]s it. is their clone a huge goyf too or just a regular one? and does the clone even know how big a goyf should be since the p/t is */*+1
rows.expected_answer: Just a regular Tarmogoyf. A copy acquires only the copiable values of the original (707.2): name, mana cost, types, rules text, printed P/T, etc. Counters, Giant Growth's +3/+3, and other non-copy effects are not copiable values, so the Clone gets none of them. The Clone does copy Tarmogoyf's rules text, and therefore its characteristic-defining ability (707.2a), so the Clone's own P/T is */*+1 computed from card types in graveyards (applied in layer 7a, 613.4a). The copy effect itself is applied in layer 1a (613.2a); your goyf's counters and pump are layer 7c (613.4c) and stay on your goyf only.

outcome.answer: Their Clone is a plain **Tarmogoyf** — same size as yours would be with no counters and no pump. It does copy the characteristic-defining ability, so it knows how big to be: copiable values are "the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty)" (`707.2`), and the CDA "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1" is rules text, so the Clone has it and computes its own */*+1 from the graveyards. What it doesn't get: counters and non-copy effects. Per `707.2`, "Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied," and Scryfall confirms Clone "doesn't copy whether that creature is tapped or untapped, whether it has any counters on it or Auras and Equipment attached to it, or any non-copy effects that have changed its power, toughness, types, color, or so on." So your **Giant Growth** and the two +1/+1 counters stay yours; if three card types are in graveyards, yours is 8/9 and theirs is 3/4.

rows.question: ok classic one. I have [[Humility]] out and my opponent drops [[Opalescence]]. what are Humility and Opalescence now?? are all my creatures still 1/1? does the answer change if Opalescence was out first?
rows.expected_answer: Walk the layers. Opalescence reads 'each OTHER non-Aura enchantment', so it never affects itself: Opalescence stays a noncreature enchantment and keeps its ability in every scenario. Layer 4 (613.1d): Opalescence makes Humility a 'creature' enchantment. Layer 6 (613.1f): Humility removes all abilities from every creature, including itself; per 613.6 an effect that has started applying keeps applying in later layers even though its source ability is gone. Layer 7b (613.4b): Humility's 'base P/T 1/1' and Opalescence's 'base P/T equal to mana value' both set Humility's P/T. Neither depends on the other under 613.8a (applying one doesn't change the text, existence, or targets of the other), so timestamp order decides (613.7). If Opalescence has the later timestamp: Humility is a 4/4 creature with no abilities. If Humility has the later timestamp: Humility is a 1/1 creature with no abilities. Either way every other creature is a 1/1 with no abilities, and Opalescence is an unaffected noncreature enchantment.

outcome.answer:
Your board: **Humility** was out first, so it ends up a 4/4 enchantment creature, **Opalescence** stays a noncreature enchantment with no power/toughness, and your ordinary creatures are 1/1 with no abilities.

Walking the layers: layer 4, Opalescence's "Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types" animates Humility (and any other non-Aura enchantments) — but it "Does not animate itself," so Opalescence isn't a creature and keeps its ability, since Humility only strips abilities from creatures. Layer 6, Humility's "All creatures lose all abilities" applies to everything that's now a creature, including Humility itself; it keeps applying in later layers even though it removed its own ability, per `613.6`. Layer 7b, both "base power and toughness 1/1" and "base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value" are P/T-setting effects in the same sublayer (`613.4b`), so the later timestamp wins (`613.7`). Humility is older, so Opalescence's setting applies last: Humility and any other animated enchantment are 4/4 (mana value 4). Normal creatures aren't touched by Opalescence, so they stay 1/1.

Reverse the order and yes, it changes: if Opalescence was already out and Humility arrives later, Humility's 1/1 has the later timestamp, so every creature — including the animated enchantments and Humility itself — is 1/1 with no abilities. Opalescence itself is still a noncreature enchantment either way.

rule 613.4b: "Layer 7b: Effects that set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value are applied."

rows.question: quick one: if I have [[Valki, God of Lies]] in hand can I just cast the Tibalt side for 7? and while it's in my library/graveyard does it count as a planeswalker card for stuff like Vraska's Contempt / Kaya's Ghostform?
rows.expected_answer: Yes. Valki // Tibalt is a modal double-faced card: when you cast it you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack, and only that face is evaluated (712.11b, 712.11c), so you can cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for {5}{B}{R} straight from your hand. Once chosen, the spell/permanent has only that face's characteristics (712.8f). But anywhere other than the stack or battlefield (hand, library, graveyard, exile) an MDFC has only its front face's characteristics (712.8a), so it is a legendary creature card named Valki, God of Lies there — never a planeswalker card.

outcome.answer:
Yes on both counts, with a catch on the second.

**Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor** is a modal double-faced card, and you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack (`712.11b`), so from hand you can cast the Tibalt face for {5}{B}{R} — seven mana. Only that face is evaluated for legality (`712.11c`).

In your library, graveyard, hand, or exile the card is *only* Valki: "While a double-faced card is outside the game or in a zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face" (`712.8a`). So it's a legendary creature card with mana value 2 there, not a planeswalker card — "In all other zones, consider only the front face."

On the battlefield it has only the characteristics of the face that's up (`712.8f`), so a resolved Tibalt is a planeswalker: **Vraska's Contempt** can target and exile it, and **Kaya's Ghostform** can be attached to it ("Enchant creature or planeswalker you control"). But when Ghostform's trigger returns the card from exile, it enters front face up by default (`712.14`) — you get Valki back, not Tibalt.
citations: rule 712.11b: "A player casting a modal double-faced card or a copy of a modal double-faced card as a spell chooses which face they are casting before putting it onto the stack."
rule 712.11c: "Only the face that will be face up on the stack is evaluated to determine if it can be cast."
rule 712.8a: "While a double-faced card is outside the game or in a zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face."
rule 712.8f: "While a modal double-faced spell is on the stack or a modal double-faced permanent is on the battlefield, it has only the characteristics of the face that’s up."
rule 712.14: "A double-faced card put onto the battlefield from a zone other than the stack enters the battlefield with its front face up by default."
ruling 907ae517-22d5-4ac7-bc3a-3f4d5eaeeb57/37339bfb61f528f0: "On the stack and battlefield, consider whichever face is up. In all other zones, consider only the front face."

rows.question: cast Stomp off my bonecrusher giant, it resolved and went to exile. my opp says I can only cast the creature half from exile now, not Stomp again, is that right? also can they counter Stomp with a 'counter target creature spell' effect since the card is a creature?
rows.expected_answer: Your opponent is right. When an Adventure spell resolves it is exiled instead of going to the graveyard, and you may cast the card from exile — but only as the creature (Bonecrusher Giant), not as Stomp again (715.3d). And no, Stomp can't be hit by 'counter target creature spell': while on the stack as an Adventure the spell has only its alternative characteristics (715.3a, 715.3b), so it is a red instant, not a creature spell. Everywhere else, including exile, the card is just the creature card Bonecrusher Giant (715.4).

outcome.answer:
Your opponent is right on both counts. **Stomp** resolved, so per `715.3d` you exiled it instead of putting it in the graveyard, and "For as long as that card remains exiled, that player may play it. It can't be cast as an Adventure this way" — so the only thing you can cast from exile is **Bonecrusher Giant**, the creature half, and only when you could normally cast a creature spell (your main phase, empty stack).

And no, a "counter target creature spell" effect can't hit Stomp. While it's on the stack as an Adventure it has only the Adventure's characteristics (`715.3b`), i.e. it's an Instant named Stomp costing {1}{R} — the Giant's creature characteristics simply aren't there. They'd need something that counters instants (or any spell). The card only goes back to its normal characteristics in other zones or when cast as the creature (`715.4`).
citations: rule 715.3d: "For as long as that card remains exiled, that player may play it. It can’t be cast as an Adventure this way"
rule 715.3b: "While on the stack as an Adventure, the spell has only its alternative characteristics."
rule 715.4: "In every zone except the stack, and while on the stack not as an Adventure, an adventurer card has only its normal characteristics."

ruling d6d72f5f-8f5d-4180-b514-f22ff5482902/e5d61736cf47758e: "You must still follow any timing restrictions and permissions for the permanent spell you cast from exile. Normally, you'll be able to cast it only during your main phase while the stack is empty."

rows.question: melded my Bruna and Gisela into Brisela and then it got Path to Exiled. does that count as one creature leaving or two for my [[Blood Artist]] type triggers, and do I get one Plains or two off Path?
rows.expected_answer:
Blood Artist does not trigger at all here: Path to Exile exiles Brisela, and Blood Artist
triggers on a creature dying, which means being put into a graveyard from the battlefield
(700.4). Exile is not dying. If Brisela instead died (say, to a Wrath of God), Blood Artist
would trigger exactly once: one permanent left the battlefield, even though the melded
permanent is a single object represented by two cards (712.21, 701.42a). A trigger reading
"whenever a card is put into a graveyard" would see two cards (712.21e). Either way, Path's
controller gets the search-for-a-Plains effect once, and Bruna and Gisela both go to exile.

outcome.answer:
No Blood Artist triggers at all, and one Plains.

**Path to Exile** exiles; it doesn't put anything in a graveyard, and **Blood Artist** only cares about a creature that "dies" — "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life." A creature that's exiled from the battlefield never dies, so nothing triggers.

Had **Brisela, Voice of Nightmares** actually died instead, it would be exactly one death trigger: "If a melded permanent leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards are put into the appropriate zone" (`712.21`), and "If an effect needs to know the number of objects that changed zones, a melded permanent among those objects counts as one object that moved" (`712.21e`). Only abilities counting *cards* hitting the graveyard (e.g. "whenever a card is put into a graveyard from anywhere") would see two.

For Path, one creature was exiled and the spell grants one search: "Its controller may search their library for a basic land card, put that card onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle." One basic land, not two. Note also that you choose the relative timestamp order of Bruna and Gisela in exile (`712.21b`).

oracle d683d985-9888-4d21-8b5f-69e69ce4a03b#0: "Its controller may search their library for a basic land card, put that card onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle."
rule 712.21: "If a melded permanent leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards are put into the appropriate zone."
rule 712.21e: "If an effect needs to know the number of objects that changed zones, a melded permanent among those objects counts as one object that moved."

rows.question: old school question. my Waylay (Urza's Saga printing) says 'at end of turn, remove them from the game'. so I cast it during my opponent's end step, the knights survive since the end step already started, and I get to swing with them on my turn right? classic waylay trick
rows.expected_answer: No — that trick was closed by errata. The printed text is not what the card does; you always use the current Oracle wording (108.1), which is 'Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step.' If you cast Waylay in your opponent's end step, the Knights are exiled at that same turn's cleanup step: the game checks for triggered abilities waiting during cleanup, puts the 'beginning of the next cleanup step' trigger on the stack, and then players get priority and another cleanup step follows (514.3a). You never get to attack with them. (Casting it during your opponent's declare-attackers step to get surprise blockers still works.)

rows.question: my mirage LED says 'play this ability as an interrupt'. so it's a mana ability and I can crack it in the middle of casting Infernal Tutor to pay for it right? that way I still have tutor as the last card when I discard
rows.expected_answer: No. Ignore the printed 'interrupt' text and use the current Oracle wording (108.1): 'Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant.' It is still a mana ability — the timing restriction doesn't change that (605.1) — but 'Activate only as an instant' means you may only activate it when you have priority (602.5e), so you can't activate it while paying for a spell the way 605.3a normally allows for mana abilities. The correct play is to cast Infernal Tutor with Tutor as the last card in hand, hold priority, then activate LED in response; when Tutor resolves you are hellbent and the mana is still floating.

outcome.answer:
No. Your Mirage copy's "play this ability as an interrupt" text is long gone — the Oracle text of **Lion's Eye Diamond** is "Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant." That last line is what stops your line.

LED's ability *is* a mana ability (`605.1` — an ability is a mana ability regardless of "what timing restrictions (such as 'Activate only as an instant') they may have"), so it doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to (`605.3b`). But "Activate only as an instant" means you must follow the timing rules for casting an instant (`602.5e`), i.e. only when you have priority and the stack is in a state where you could cast an instant. You never have priority in the middle of casting **Infernal Tutor**, so the window 601.2g normally gives you to activate mana abilities while paying costs isn't available to LED.

So you can't crack LED to pay for Tutor. The actual line is: cast Infernal Tutor with other mana, keep priority after it's cast, then activate LED — your hand is now empty (Tutor is on the stack, not in hand), so hellbent is satisfied on resolution, and the three mana sits in your pool for the rest of the step.

rule 601.2g: "601.2g If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, “Mana Abilities”). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid."

rows.question: ok so I have [[Blood Artist]] out and my opponent wraths with [[Wrath of God]]. Blood Artist dies at the same time as everything else so does it even see the other creatures die? do I drain for all of them or just itself?
rows.expected_answer: Yes, you drain for every creature that died, including Blood Artist itself. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities 'look back in time' (603.10, 603.6c): the game checks the state immediately before the event, when Blood Artist was still on the battlefield, so it sees every creature that died simultaneously, including itself. All those triggers go on the stack the next time a player would receive priority (603.3), and you choose a target player for each one.

outcome.answer:
You drain for every creature that died, including **Blood Artist** itself. If **Wrath of God** kills Blood Artist plus N other creatures, you get N+1 triggers: each one has a target player lose 1 life and you gain 1 life.

Blood Artist reads "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life." That's a dies (leaves-the-battlefield) trigger, and those look back in time — the game uses the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event, so Blood Artist is still there with its ability for the trigger check (`603.10`, `603.10a`). The example printed under `603.10` is exactly this case: an artifact with "Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life" triggers twice when it's destroyed alongside two creatures. And one event containing multiple occurrences triggers the ability repeatedly (`603.2c`).

Each trigger targets independently, so you pick targets for all of them as they go on the stack.
citations: rule 603.10: "the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event"
rule 603.10a: "Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities"
rule 603.10: "The artifact’s ability triggers twice, even though the artifact goes to its owner’s graveyard at the same time as the creatures."
rule 603.2c: "An ability triggers only once each time its trigger event occurs. However, it can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences."
oracle 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d#0: "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life."
ruling 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d/eaf0e0e76c3621ab: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."

rows.question: my buddy says once I cast a spell he can't respond until I 'pass'. I cast Lightning Bolt at his bob, do I get to keep going and cast a second Bolt before he gets a chance to counter the first one?
rows.expected_answer: Your buddy is half right. After you cast a spell you receive priority again (117.3c), so you may cast the second Bolt immediately, before he can respond to the first. He only gets priority when you pass. Nothing resolves until all players pass in succession with the stack non-empty (117.4); then only the top object resolves, and the active player gets priority again after it resolves (117.3b). So he can still respond to either Bolt once you pass, but you are entitled to stack both first.

outcome.answer:
Your buddy is half right, and you're right about the rest. After you cast a spell you keep priority (`117.3c`: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward"), so you may cast a second **Lightning Bolt** immediately, before he ever gets a chance to act. He only gets priority once you pass it (`117.4`), and nothing resolves until all players pass in succession.

But holding priority doesn't protect the first Bolt. When you finally pass, he gets priority with both Bolts on the stack and can respond to either one — the counterspell he casts then resolves first (`117.7`), and the stack resolves top-down, last in first out (`405.2`).

One trap: if both Bolts target the same **Dark Confidant**, the second one you cast is on top and resolves first. If it kills the Confidant, the first Bolt has no legal target left and is removed from the stack without effect (`608.2b`) — you can't stack two Bolts at one creature and expect one to "carry over" to something else.
citations: rule 117.3c: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward."
rule 117.4: "If all players pass in succession (that is, if all players pass without taking any actions in between passing), the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves"

rule 117.7: "If a player with priority casts a spell or activates an activated ability while another spell or ability is already on the stack, the new spell or ability has been cast or activated “in response to” t…"
rule 405.2: "Each time an object is put on the stack, it’s put on top of all objects already there."

rule 608.2b: "If all its targets, for every instance of the word “target,” are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn’t resolve. It’s removed from the stack and, if it’s a spell, put into its owner’s graveyard."

rows.question: I control a 2/2 with a Giant Growth resolving on it, and mid-resolution of a different spell it's technically at 0 toughness for a second (Maro-style hand-size thing). Does it die? And separately, if I have two Ragavan on the battlefield somehow, when exactly does the legend rule kick in - can I respond in between?
rows.expected_answer: 1) It doesn't die. State-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority, not in the middle of a spell resolving (704.3, 704.4 - the CR's own Maro example). The creature only dies if it still has toughness 0 or less when SBAs are next checked (704.5f). 2) The legend rule (704.5j) is also a state-based action: the moment a player would get priority with two Ragavans you control, you choose one and the other goes to the graveyard. It doesn't use the stack and there is no window to respond between the second Ragavan entering and the legend rule applying; you can only respond before the second one enters/resolves.

outcome.answer:
**No, it doesn't die.** State-based actions are only checked when a player would get priority, and they "pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability" (`704.4`). Toughness dipping to 0 in the middle of a resolution is irrelevant as long as it's back above 0 when the spell finishes; only then is `704.5f` checked ("If a creature has toughness 0 or less, it's put into its owner's graveyard"). The same holds if **Giant Growth** is what props it up — once it has resolved, the +3/+3 is applied continuously, so at the next SBA check the creature has positive toughness.

**On the legend rule: no, there's no window to respond.** It's a state-based action (`704.5j`): if two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one and the rest go to their owners' graveyards. SBAs don't use the stack (`704.1`) and are performed before any player receives priority (`117.5`), and the check repeats until nothing more happens. So the moment the second **Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer** hits the battlefield and someone would get priority, one of them is put into the graveyard first — nobody can respond "in between" having two and losing one. (You can of course respond to the spell/ability that would put the second one onto the battlefield, before it happens.)
citations: ruling ef32258a-d567-4fbc-ab85-8c00080f5b36/654c63e82671903c: "If Maro’s toughness goes to 0 during the announcement or resolution of a spell or ability and then goes back up above 0 before the end of that announcement or resolution, it won’t be put into your gra…"
rule 704.4: "Unlike triggered abilities, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability."
rule 704.5f: "If a creature has toughness 0 or less, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard."
rule 704.5j: "If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards."
rule 117.5: "Each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event"
rule 704.1: "State-based actions don’t use the stack."

rows.question: I attack with a 5/5 trample that also has deathtouch (Questing Beast) and they block with a 4/4. how much can I trample over? my opponent says I have to assign 4 to the blocker first
rows.expected_answer: You only need to assign 1 damage to the 4/4 and can trample 4 over to the player. Trample requires lethal damage to be assigned to all blockers before excess goes to the player (702.19b), but any nonzero damage from a deathtouch source counts as lethal for that purpose (702.2c). Damage assignment for a blocked creature follows 510.1c, then all combat damage is dealt simultaneously with no chance to respond in between (510.2). The 4/4 is then destroyed by deathtouch as an SBA.

outcome.answer:
Two corrections first: **Questing Beast** is a 4/4, not a 5/5, and it has no trample — its Oracle text reads "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste" plus the can't-be-blocked-by-power-2-or-less, damage-can't-be-prevented, and planeswalker-damage abilities. With no trample, a blocked Questing Beast assigns all 4 of its combat damage to the single blocker and nothing goes through: "If exactly one creature is blocking it, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature" (`510.1c`).

If the attacker did have trample alongside deathtouch, your opponent would be wrong: you assign lethal damage to the blockers first, then the excess where you like (`702.19b`), and with deathtouch "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt" (`702.2c`). So a 5/5 trample+deathtouch attacker blocked by a 4/4 assigns just 1 to the blocker and 4 to the player.
citations: oracle b685757b-521e-4353-a233-97052359723d#0: "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste"
rule 510.1c: "If exactly one creature is blocking it, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature."

rule 702.19b: "The controller of an attacking creature with trample first assigns damage to the creature(s) blocking it. Once all those blocking creatures are assigned lethal damage, any excess damage is assigned as…"

rule 702.2c: "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt."

rows.question: commander q: my commander is [[Kenrith, the Returned King]]. two things: 1) can I run Nicol Bolas, the Ravager since Kenrith's text mentions all 5 colors? and 2) someone bounced Kenrith to my hand with Unsummon - does he go to the command zone or is that only for graveyard/exile?
rows.expected_answer: 1) Yes. Color identity includes mana symbols in the mana cost AND in the rules text (903.4), so Kenrith's identity is WUBRG even though his mana cost is only {4}{W}. Nicol Bolas, the Ravager (UBR) is legal because every color in its identity is in Kenrith's (903.5c). 2) Yes, Kenrith can go to the command zone. If a commander would be put into its owner's hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead - a replacement effect (903.9b). Graveyard/exile use a separate state-based action (903.9a). Either way it's optional.

outcome.answer:
Both answers are yes.

1) **Kenrith, the Returned King**'s color identity is all five colors: color identity is "the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card's mana cost or rules text" (`903.4`), and Kenrith's rules text includes "{R}: All creatures gain trample and haste until end of turn." along with the {1}{G}, {2}{W}, {3}{U} and {4}{B} activation costs, on top of his white mana cost — WUBRG. **Nicol Bolas, the Ravager // Nicol Bolas, the Arisen** is blue-black-red (front face's mana cost, plus the back face's color indicator, which counts per `903.4d`), so every color in its identity is in Kenrith's and it's legal under `903.5c`. A five-color commander lets you run essentially anything.

2) Command zone, if you want it there. The graveyard/exile state-based action in `903.9a` isn't the only route: `903.9b` says "If a commander would be put into its owner's hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead." **Unsummon** returning Kenrith to your hand is exactly that event, so you may apply the replacement — he'll then cost {2} more the next time you cast him from there per `903.8`. You may also just let him go to your hand.
citations: ruling d209b948-9afb-4fd1-a961-72c87282878c/e4f2be13783d5f46: "Kenrith's first ability affects only creatures on the battlefield at the time it resolves."
oracle d209b948-9afb-4fd1-a961-72c87282878c#0: "{R}: All creatures gain trample and haste until end of turn."
rule 903.4: "The color identity of a card is the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card’s mana cost or rules text"
rule 903.4d: "The back face of a double-faced card (see rule 712) is included when determining a card’s color identity."
ruling 55e4b27e-5447-4fc2-8cae-a03e344600c6/3912077524ea798e: "Nicol Bolas, the Arisen has a color indicator on its typeline. This color indicator means that it's a blue, black, and red permanent."
rule 903.5c: "A card can be included in a Commander deck only if every color in its color identity is also found in the color identity of the deck’s commander."
rule 903.9b: "If a commander would be put into its owner’s hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead."
rule 903.8: "A commander cast from the command zone costs an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game."

rows.question: commander damage question. I've been hit for 15 by my opponent's Rafiq. she then copies it with a Clone and hits me for 6 more with the clone. do I lose? also does the 21 count noncombat damage like from Fling?
rows.expected_answer: No to both. A player loses when they've been dealt 21 or more COMBAT damage by the SAME commander over the course of the game (903.10a; checked as a state-based action, 704.6c). The Clone copying Rafiq is not a commander, so its 6 damage isn't commander damage - you're still at 15 from the real Rafiq. Fling damage is noncombat, so it never counts toward the 21 either; it just reduces your life total normally.

outcome.answer:
You don't lose, and no — only combat damage from an actual commander counts.

Being a commander is an attribute of the card, not a copiable characteristic: per `903.3`, "This designation is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself," and "A permanent that’s copying a commander (such as a Body Double, for example, copying a commander in a player’s graveyard) is not a commander." So the **Clone** is just a Rafiq-shaped creature and its 6 damage is ordinary combat damage. You're at 15 from **Rafiq of the Many** and nothing else tracks against him. (Even if the Clone somehow were a commander, `903.10a` counts damage from "the same commander," so the two totals still wouldn't add.)

As for **Fling**: the state-based action is "A player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game" (`903.10a`, also `104.3j`). Fling's damage isn't combat damage, so it costs you life normally but never counts toward the 21.
citations: rule 903.3: "This designation is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself."
rule 903.3: "A permanent that’s copying a commander (such as a Body Double, for example, copying a commander in a player’s graveyard) is not a commander."
rule 903.10a: "A player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game."
rule 104.3j: "In a Commander game, a player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game."

rows.question: two quick ones. 1) if I tap all my lands during my upkeep does that mana stick around so I can cast the mind sculptor in my main phase? 2) when I'm casting snappy can I tap lands in the middle of casting it or do I have to float the mana first?
rows.expected_answer: 1) No. Each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, so mana added during your upkeep is lost before your main phase (106.4). Tap the lands in your main phase instead. 2) Yes. Casting a spell includes a step where, if the total cost includes mana, you get a chance to activate mana abilities such as tapping lands (601.2g), and only then do you pay the total cost (601.2h). You do not need to float mana before announcing the spell.

outcome.answer:
**1) No.** Mana doesn't survive the step. Per `106.4`, "Each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and the player is said to lose this mana." Mana floated in your upkeep is gone at the end of the upkeep step (and you'd still have the draw step to cross), so it can't pay for **Jace, the Mind Sculptor** in your main phase.

**2) You can tap mid-cast.** The normal sequence is to announce the spell, lock in the total cost, then produce mana: `601.2g` says "If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities... Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid." And `605.3a` lets you activate a mana ability "whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment... even if it's in the middle of casting or resolving a spell." Pre-floating for **Snapcaster Mage** is legal too, just unnecessary — and if you float too much, the excess is announced and then lost at end of step/phase.
citations: rule 106.4: "Each player’s mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and the player is said to lose this mana."

rule 601.2g: "If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, “Mana Abilities”). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid."

rule 605.3a: "A player may activate an activated mana ability whenever they have priority, whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment, or whenever a rule or effect asks …"
rule 106.4b: "If a player passes priority (see rule 117) while there is mana in their mana pool, that player announces what mana is there."

rows.question: my opp has [[bob]] and flipped a tim off the top, then next turn he flipped a goyf. how much life does he lose each time? goyf is like a 5/6 rn so is it 5?
rows.expected_answer: Dark Confidant makes you lose life equal to the revealed card's mana value, which is the total mana in its mana cost regardless of color (202.3). Prodigal Sorcerer costs {2}{U}, so he loses 3 life. Tarmogoyf costs {1}{G}, so he loses 2 life. Tarmogoyf's power/toughness is irrelevant; mana value is based only on the mana cost.

outcome.answer: Three, then two. Mana value is the total mana in the card's mana cost (`202.3`): **Prodigal Sorcerer** costs {2}{U}, so mana value 3; **Tarmogoyf** costs {1}{G}, so mana value 2 — no matter how big it is on the battlefield. Tarmogoyf's characteristic-defining ability ("Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1") sets power and toughness, which has nothing to do with its mana cost (`208.2a`). So **Dark Confidant** has him "reveal the top card of your library and put that card into your hand. You lose life equal to its mana value" — 3 life for the Tim, 2 for the Goyf.
citations: rule 202.3: "The mana value of an object is a number equal to the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color."
rule 208.2a: "The card may have a characteristic-defining ability that sets its power and/or toughness according to some stated condition."
oracle 45900b2f-f6a9-4c42-9642-008f3c1cf6dd#0: "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1."
oracle 5e961d15-5972-4e4b-9385-1cd7cd7c6bbe#0: "{T}: This creature deals 1 damage to any target."
oracle 2068185c-1b50-47d0-aa3f-bf505d199428#0: "reveal the top card of your library and put that card into your hand. You lose life equal to its mana value."
